topic: 3-minute checklist: how Westchester homeowners can spot a failing boiler before February
text:
Most boiler failures we respond to in February weren't surprises — the warning signs were there in November.

After years of servicing homes across Westchester County, our technicians have noticed the same pattern: homeowners assume a boiler that's "mostly working" will keep working. Then the coldest week of winter arrives and it doesn't.

Here's a quick 3-minute check any homeowner can do right now:

1. Look at your pressure gauge. A properly operating hot-water boiler should read between 12–25 psi. Consistently low or spiking pressure points to a leak, a failing expansion tank, or a faulty pressure-relief valve — none of which fix themselves.

2. Listen during a heat cycle. Banging, kettling, or gurgling sounds from the boiler or pipes often mean sediment buildup, trapped air, or a circulator pump that's on its way out. A quiet boiler is a healthy boiler.

3. Check your pilot light or burner flame (if accessible). On gas equipment, a steady blue flame is normal. A yellow or orange flame, or one that flickers and dies, can signal combustion issues that go beyond inconvenience.

4. Note your fuel consumption. If you're burning noticeably more oil or gas than last winter for the same level of comfort, efficiency has dropped — and that usually means a component is struggling.

5. Look for water. Any moisture around the boiler base, on supply lines, or near the expansion tank deserves a professional look before it becomes a flooded basement in January.

None of this requires tools. It takes three minutes and can save a homeowner a 2 a.m. emergency call in the middle of a Westchester cold snap.

For HVAC and plumbing professionals: what's the most common boiler symptom your customers ignored until it was too late? We'd genuinely like to hear what you're seeing in the field.

topic: 3-minute checklist: how Westchester homeowners can spot a failing boiler before February
text:
Hey neighbors — with the cold settling in across Westchester County, I wanted to share a quick checklist our team put together for homeowners with boilers. These are the warning signs we most commonly see before a system gives out in the middle of winter.

Take three minutes and walk through these:

🔹 Pressure gauge reading — A hot-water boiler should hold steady between 12 and 25 psi. If yours is creeping low or spiking, that's worth looking into now rather than in February.

🔹 Unusual sounds — Banging, gurgling, or a low rumbling (sometimes called "kettling") during a heat cycle often means sediment buildup or a circulator pump that's struggling. A boiler running quietly is usually a boiler running well.

🔹 Flame color — If you can see the burner, the flame should be blue. Yellow or orange flames on gas equipment can indicate a combustion issue.

🔹 Any water around the unit — Moisture near the boiler base, the expansion tank, or the supply lines isn't normal. Even a slow drip can turn into a bigger problem once the system is working harder in deep winter.

🔹 Higher-than-usual fuel bills — If you're spending noticeably more on oil or gas but your home isn't any warmer, efficiency has dropped and something is likely working harder than it should.

You don't need any tools for any of this — just a few minutes before the temperatures really drop.

We're Bravo Mechanical, and we've been servicing boilers and heating systems throughout Westchester County for years. Happy to answer questions in the comments if anything on that list sounds familiar in your home.

topic: How Westchester homeowners can prep their boilers for winter — a 5-minute checklist
text:
Most boiler failures we see in November and December weren't sudden — they were slow-building problems that a quick pre-season check would have caught in October.

Westchester winters hit hard, and cast-iron boilers, in particular, don't forgive neglect. Before you fire yours up for the season, here's a 5-minute checklist worth running through:

1. Check the pressure gauge — it should read between 12–15 psi at rest. Anything lower often signals a slow leak or a waterlogged expansion tank.
2. Bleed your baseboard radiators or cast-iron sections if you hear banging or uneven heat last winter.
3. Look at the pilot or ignition area for soot buildup — that's a combustion efficiency problem, not just cosmetic.
4. Confirm your low-water cutoff is clean. A clogged LWCO won't protect your boiler if water drops dangerously low.
5. Test your thermostat by calling for heat now, before you actually need it at midnight in January.

At Bravo Mechanical, we serve homeowners across Westchester County — from older homes in Yonkers and Mount Vernon with decades-old Weil-McLain systems to newer builds in Pleasantville running high-efficiency Burnham boilers. The equipment varies. The pre-season discipline shouldn't.

If your boiler hasn't had a professional tune-up in the last 12 months, now is the right time — not after the first cold snap when our schedule fills up.
